extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, critics, and educated readers interested in drama and poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for judging or composing drama, comedy, and poetry — covering unity, characterization, moral tone, language, theatrical effects, and issues of translation and metre. Aimed at identifying what makes works intellectually and aesthetically satisfying rather than merely popular or sensational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance satire with human kindness
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire should include a conciliatory or humane element so that ridicule does not degenerate into contempt or hatred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (Hogarth): introduce a beautiful, tender central figure amid humorous deformities to 'diffuse through all... a spirit of reconciliation and human kindness' so that laughter remains instructive rather than heart-poisoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and unity of the work
rubrics_metrics.description: A dramatic piece should preserve 'a fitness in the parts, and a harmony in the whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: French tragedies praised as 'consistent works of art' — even if they form a 'false nature', coherence of structure and parts is essential to the work's artistic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stimulate active thought and aim at ideal excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should excite the mind to active thought and lead spectators/readers to strive after higher, ideal excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good drama and tragedy do not merely produce sensation; they provoke reflection and ennoblement of the imagination ('transport the mind to a sense of its possible greatness').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stupefying mere sensation or empty sensational curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on shocking or sensational incidents that produce mere feeling without dignity or intellectual engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical contrast with 'worthless sympathy with our own ordinary sufferings' or 'an empty curiosity for the surprising' — language and situations must dignify the imagination, not stupefy it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involution of the universal in the individual (universality through particularization)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet/ playwright should embody universal truths within distinct individual characters ('an involution of the universal in the individual').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotelian ideal: in poetry the individual form in which truth is clothed should make the universal evident through a single, particular character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularize class-characteristics to create individuality and instructiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Class-characteristics should be modified and particularized in each person, so that characters feel individual and instructive rather than merely types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'instructiveness of a character' comes from particularized class traits applied to distinct persons (e.g., Shakespeare's Jaques, Falstaff, fools — class-based yet individualized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject cheap comedic devices and maudlin pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid relying on wry faces, jargon, slang phrases, or melodramatic tears to provoke laughter or tears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include 'wry faces, accidents of jargon, slang phrases' and 'the maudlin tears of drunkenness' — comedy and tragedy should derive from character and language, not cheap tricks or sentimental excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage understanding and imagination within pleasurable effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic scenes should affect the audience within the bounds of pleasure and in union with intellectual and imaginative activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to 'implant the germs of that greatness' and to raise the mind during the experience rather than overwhelm or merely distress it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sentimental morality that flatters without demanding virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Moralizing sentiment that comforts the audience and requires no real sacrifice is a defect — it flatters vices rather than cultivates virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentimental plays that send one 'away pleased with your own hearts, and quite reconciled to your vices' are condemned; morality in drama should be demanding and truthful, not self-congratulatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer lofty subjects and high dramatic stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama should represent 'human nature in its height and vigour' and be capable of involving great interests (e.g., dependence of thousands on the fate of one).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low, pettifogging subjects or strictly domestic petty concerns lack the scale to evoke the sublime emotions proper to tragedy; the poet should aim for actions with significant consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value manner, language, and treatment over mere novelty of incident
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness often lies in the treatment — the poet's manner and language — more than in original plots; familiar or 'stock' stories can become extraordinary through superior handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare often used pre-existing stories; his excellence derived from his language, characterization, and dramatic handling rather than novelty of plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contrived plots that simply gratify audience expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots that make 'everything turn out exactly as we would wish' and gratify audience prejudices are artistically inferior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictable, consolatory endings that merely confirm audience biases (and thereby flatter them) reduce dramatic power; surprise should not replace truthful depiction of causes and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-rely on theatrical trickery or sensory gimmicks
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on loud explosions, smells, or other stage effects can create striking moments but are poor substitutes for genuine dramatic naturalness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a deafening explosion and real gunpowder smell created 'naturalness' of scene for spectators but is implied as an inadequate substitute for substantive dramatic craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware dramatic popularity gained by moral inversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Popularity that arises from subverting natural order — rewarding criminals or rewarding inversion of expected moral relations — is dangerous and suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author faults dramas that excite audiences by representing virtues in unlikely persons and by rewarding the criminally disposed with sympathy, calling such 'moral and intellectual Jacobinism.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Verse harmony: cadences, pauses, and the sweep of paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmonious verse depends on the arrangement of pauses and cadences and the sweep of whole paragraphs rather than an even flow or isolated striking lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted ideal: the English iambic blank verse's excellence lies in 'apt arrangement of pauses and cadences, and the sweep of whole paragraphs, "with many a winding bout / Of linked sweetness long drawn out,"' while prominence of single lines is injurious except when used purposefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge language constraints in translation and metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Different languages have different capacities for concision and line-equivalence; translations must respect these natural limits (e.g., German may compress meaning into a single line more readily than English).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Klopstock's claim that 'a German line proved always sufficient for a Greek or Latin one' is contrasted with the English need for more space; translators should be aware that metre and linguistic structure constrain literal line-for-line rendering.
